title: Text Processing Pipelines
intro: The real power of the Linux shell is chaining small tools with pipes. Let's answer a real question from an nginx access log: which IPs are hammering us, and with what?

steps.prompt: Show only the lines in access.log that are NOT successful 200 responses.
steps.explanation: -v inverts the match — show lines that DON'T contain the pattern.
steps.why: The spaces around 200 matter: without them, grep -v '200' would also drop a 500 response whose byte count happened to contain '200'. Precise patterns avoid silently wrong answers.

steps.prompt: Print just the first column (the client IP) from every line.
steps.explanation: awk splits each line on whitespace; $1 is the first field.
steps.why: 'cut -d' ' -f1' works here too, but awk handles multiple consecutive spaces correctly and can do arithmetic/conditions later — it's the more general tool once you know it.

steps.prompt: Now count requests per IP and show the top offenders, highest first.
steps.explanation: sort groups identical lines together, uniq -c counts each group, sort -rn orders by that count numerically, descending.
steps.why: uniq only collapses ADJACENT duplicates — that's why the first sort is mandatory. Forgetting it is the most common mistake with this pipeline and gives wrong counts silently.

steps.prompt: Add 'head' to show only the top 3.
expected_commands: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
steps.explanation: 203.0.113.9 made 50x more requests than anyone else — likely a scraper or an attack.
steps.why: This exact pipeline (extract a field → sort → uniq -c → sort -rn → head) is one of the most reused patterns in operations work. Once it's muscle memory, you can answer 'top N of anything' from any log in seconds.

steps.prompt: Replace every occurrence of 'staging-db' with 'prod-db' in config.env, printing the result without modifying the file.
steps.explanation: s/old/new/g substitutes all matches on each line; without -i, sed prints the result and leaves the file untouched.
steps.why: Always run sed WITHOUT -i first to preview the change — then add -i to apply it once you've confirmed the output. An in-place sed with a wrong pattern can silently corrupt a config file.

steps.prompt: Compare the old and new config files to see exactly what differs.
steps.explanation: < lines are from the first file, > lines from the second.
steps.why: Diffing against a backup before restarting a service is a cheap way to confirm you changed exactly what you meant to, and nothing else.
